text: Take a photograph and add a little static, then a little more, and keep going until nothing is left but noise. Destroying an image this way is trivial. The idea behind diffusion models, which goes back to Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues in twenty fifteen, is that if a network can learn to undo one small step of that destruction, then running it backwards many times can turn pure noise into a new image.

The forward process is fixed, not learned. In the paper that made the approach work well, by Ho, Jain and Abbeel in twenty twenty, there are a thousand steps. At each one, the image is shrunk slightly toward zero and a small amount of Gaussian noise is added, following a schedule of noise levels called beta. The shrinking keeps the overall scale under control, so that after enough steps the result is indistinguishable from standard normal noise.

A convenient fact makes training cheap. Because Gaussian noise added to Gaussian noise is still Gaussian, you can jump from the clean image to any step in a single move: the square root of alpha bar times the clean image, plus the square root of one minus alpha bar times fresh noise, where alpha bar is the product of all the one-minus-beta factors so far. Early steps keep most of the image and late steps keep almost none, like a radio signal fading under rising static.

Training then becomes a simple regression. Pick a clean image, a random step and a random noise sample, build the noisy version in one move, and ask the network to predict the noise that was added, scored by the squared error. Ho and colleagues found that this simplified objective, predicting the noise rather than the image, gave their best samples, even though it drops the weights that the full derivation would put on each step.

To generate, start from pure noise at the last step. At every step, the network's estimate of the noise is used to move toward a cleaner image: remove a scaled amount of the predicted noise, rescale, and add back a little fresh noise, which keeps the process from collapsing onto a blurry average. A thousand such steps from static to picture made the original method slow, and later samplers cut the number of steps considerably.

Why should predicting noise produce images? The predicted noise points away from the region where real images live, so subtracting it is like following an arrow on a hillside that always points uphill, toward more probable images. That connects diffusion to score matching, the idea of learning the direction in which data becomes more likely, which Song and Ermon developed for image generation at around the same time.

To control what is generated, the network also receives a description, such as a text embedding, and a technique called classifier-free guidance strengthens its influence. Diffusion models overtook GANs on standard image benchmarks, as Dhariwal and Nichol reported in a paper titled Diffusion Models Beat GANs, and combined with the latent space trick from the previous lesson, they became the basis of many of today's image generators.

So a diffusion model learns one humble skill, removing a little noise, and repeats it until an image appears. The next lesson looks at the approach that diffusion overtook, a contest between two networks: generative adversarial networks.
